I begin this reassessment by first outlining Fichte’s account of political economy and nationhood. I then discuss the scholarship on fascism and national socialism more generally, with a particular focus on the theories of three scholars—Roger Griffin, Roger Eatwell, and Zeev Sternhell. I then analyse Fichte’s views on three central topics—the economy, Germany, and anti-Semitism—and conclude that, on the basis of the scholarly insights on fascism, Fichte was not a proto-fascist, though certain aspects of his writing and his style had a strong appeal to fascists.

However, the political implications of his philosophy have dual aspects. The first is his own political theory presented in accordance with his philosophical principles.
extra_snippets: German idealist philosopher J. G. Fichte (1762‐1814), as an heir to Kant, sought to uniformity of reason in his own philosophical system Wissenschaftslehre. However, the political implications of his philosophy have dual aspects. The first is his own political theory presented in accordance with his philosophical principles.

The second is a set of political influences concerning his practical position together with his philosophy. By and large it has been the second aspect that Fichte’s nationalistic perspectives were interpreted upon. So the political implications of his philosophy have been frequently reduced as a prophet of ethnic German nationalism and Nazism.
